The keeper cooked soup on a coal stove, mended nets for the fishermen below, read almanacs and tide tables by lamplight, and wrote letters to his sister inland that often arrived weeks late. One November night the wind rose to a gale, the sea broke over the lower rocks, rain hammered the lantern glass, and a fishing boat lost its bearings near the reef. He lit the auxiliary beacon, sounded the foghorn in long steady blasts, and guided the crew safely into the cove where they anchored until dawn. The next morning the sailors thanked him with bread, cheese, dried fish, salted pork, coffee, lamp oil, rope, canvas, nails, soap, and news from the distant harbor towns. He shared his meal with the shipwrecked cat, repaired the broken shutter hinge, repainted the doorframe, swept the stairwell, replaced a cracked pane, oiled the winch, coiled the spare halyard, and entered every detail in his careful hand. Years passed in this steady rhythm of work, weather, patience, solitude, duty, hunger, cold, fog, rain, wind, calm, dawn, dusk, gulls, tides, stars, ships, bells, horns, lamps, oil, glass, iron, stone, salt, and silence, until at last the inspector arrived from the city and praised the brightest light on the coast.
